samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि च तानि भूतानि च, तेषु
samasa.sense: in every living being without exception
the power belonging to Viṣṇu, the name under which the gods began to praise her (5.7)

morph.note: Past participle of the curādi root √शब्द् (stem शब्दय-): the -ay- drops and the participle takes the connecting vowel i (शब्द् + इ + त). Used as a finite verb: ‘(is) called’.
Dative of the feminine pronoun तद्, the correlative of या: ‘to her (who …)’. नमः governs the dative of the one honoured; the verb अस्तु is understood.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु विष्णुमाया इति शब्दिता, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः नमः (अस्तु)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या देवी … शब्दिता) and its correlative in the dative (तस्यै), governed by the repeated नमः. The pattern is the same in every yā devī stanza.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who in all beings is called ‘Viṣṇumāyā’ — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who in all beings is named Viṣṇu’s Māyā: homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.

comm.t: The first of the yā devī stanzas, the most recited part of the hymn. Each names one form under which the Goddess is present in every being and answers it with a threefold salutation. The series opens with the name the gods used when they began (विष्णुमाया, 5.7), and its first verb, शब्दिता, is about naming: she is what she is called in all beings.

In the Gita Press count each नमस्तस्यै is a separate mantra, so each yā devī stanza is three mantras; the chapter’s colophon counts 66 such mantras, 22 stanzas (5.14–76 and 5.78–80). The Goddess was first named Viṣṇu’s power in chapter 1, as the Yoganidrā that holds Viṣṇu and the Mahāmāyā of Hari (1.54–55).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name, 339, विष्णुमाया. The shared title is part of a common Śākta vocabulary; the texts are separate.

sandhi.note: ā + i → e (चेतनेति); then the i of इति before a becomes y (इत्यभि-).
Visarga before t becomes s; the same in all three नमस्तस्यै.

samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि च तानि भूतानि च, तेषु

morph.note: Passive present of अभि + √धा: before the passive -ya- the root’s ā becomes ī (धीयते). अभि-√धा ‘to name’, passive ‘is called’.
From the causative stem of √चित् ‘to perceive’ (चेतय-) with -anā: ‘awareness, the state of being conscious’.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु चेतना इति अभिधीयते, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः नमः (अस्तु)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या देवी … संस्थिता) and its correlative in the dative (तस्यै), governed by the repeated नमः; the same frame as 5.14-16.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who in all beings is called ‘consciousness’ — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who in all beings is called Consciousness: homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.

comm.t: The second stanza moves from a title to what makes a being a being at all: awareness. Like the first it is a stanza of naming (अभिधीयते, ‘is called’); from the next stanza on the verb is संस्थिता and the formula …रूपेण, ‘abides in the form of’.
The series ends where this stanza begins, with consciousness: in 5.78–80 she is the one who, in the form of citi (चितिरूपेण), pervades the whole world.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 417, चेतनारूपा, ‘whose form is consciousness’, and 362, चितिः. The idea is shared; the works are distinct.

sandhi.note: The m of the prefix सम् becomes anusvāra before स.
Visarga before t becomes s; the same in all three नमस्तस्यै.

samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि च तानि भूतानि च, तेषु

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (avadhāraṇa: the first member is the form itself)
samasa.literal: by the form that is intelligence
samasa.alt: Also a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, बुद्धेः रूपम्, ‘the form of …’; the karmadhāraya fits the series, where she is that state itself.

morph.note: Past participle of सम् + √स्था: before the participle -ta the root’s ā becomes i (स्थित). The m of सम् is written as anusvāra before स. The participle serves as the verb: ‘abides, is established’.

Instrumental of manner: ‘by way of the form of intelligence’, i.e. ‘as intelligence’. The n of the ending becomes ṇ after the r of रूप (internal retroflexion). The same construction runs through the following stanzas.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु बुद्धिरूपेण संस्थिता, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः नमः (अस्तु)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या देवी … संस्थिता) and its correlative in the dative (तस्यै), governed by the repeated नमः; the same frame as 5.14-16.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of intelligence — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as Intelligence: homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.

comm.t: The formula that carries the rest of the series appears here: …रूपेण संस्थिता, ‘abides in the form of …’. The first such form is बुद्धि, the understanding that discerns and decides.

The Devī Māhātmya returns to the line itself in the Nārāyaṇī hymn: सर्वस्य बुद्धिरूपेण जनस्य हृदि संस्थिते (11.8). Brahmā’s hymn had already called her बुद्धिः, ‘intelligence, whose mark is awakening’ (1.79).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the related name 223, महाबुद्धिः. The works are separate.

samasa.alt: Also a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, निद्रायाः रूपम्, ‘the form of …’; the karmadhāraya fits the series, where she is that state itself.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु निद्रारूपेण संस्थिता, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः नमः (अस्तु)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या देवी … संस्थिता) and its correlative in the dative (तस्यै), governed by the repeated नमः; the same frame as 5.14-16.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of sleep — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as Sleep: homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.

comm.t: After intelligence, sleep: the state in which understanding is withdrawn is also a form of the Goddess. The series does not praise only what is noble; it finds her in every condition of a living being.
The name recalls the first story, where the Goddess is Viṣṇu’s Yoganidrā, the sleep that holds the god until she withdraws (1.54, 1.69–71). Here the same power is present as sleep in all beings.
